tagline: A port city’s waterfront, a preserved battleship and a history of dispossession.
intro: The Cape Fear Historic Byway is part of North Carolina’s scenic-byway network. Its Wilmington setting is a port city between the Cape Fear River and the Atlantic Ocean. Downtown’s riverwalk extends 1.75 miles, with the battleship North Carolina moored across from the port area.

Water and rail once connected this city’s commerce: the Wilmington and Raleigh Railroad opened a 161-mile line to Weldon in 1840. Union Station opened at Front and Red Cross streets in 1913. Passenger service ended in 1968; the station was demolished in 1970.

Along the downtown waterfront, the battleship provides a surviving link to World War II. South of the historic downtown is Sunset Park, a neighborhood planned with views toward the Cape Fear River and Greenfield Lake. Its early houses occupy Northern and Central boulevards, while Cape Cod and ranch houses from the 1940s and 1950s line the cross streets.

moments.title: 1898 Memorial Park
moments.text: In 1898, white supremacists overthrew Wilmington’s elected government. Black residents had held public offices and worked as skilled craftspeople; Alexander and Frank Manly owned the Wilmington Daily Record. A white mob attacked and burned the newspaper, and Alfred M. Waddell’s men forced elected officials to resign at gunpoint. Waddell became mayor through the newly installed board of aldermen, and prominent Black residents and white Republicans were banished in the following days. Black residents were killed, and more than 2,100 Black people permanently left Wilmington after the attacks. Subsequent state voter-registration barriers effectively disenfranchised most Black voters.

moments.title: Battleship North Carolina
moments.text: North Carolina reached Wilmington under tow in 1961, but its arrival included a collision with a floating seafood restaurant after the tugs lost control. The battleship had faced scrapping before James Craig organized a preservation campaign and persuaded Governor Luther H. Hodges to seek a delay. It opened as a memorial in April 1962 to more than 11,000 North Carolinians who died in U.S. military service during World War II. A walkway installed in 2018 lets visitors view the ship from all sides. The walkway sits on the cofferdam built for hull repairs, allowing the ship’s structure to be repaired in place.

moments.title: Greenfield Park
moments.text: Greenfield Lake figured in plans for the Sunset Park development. In 1912, the developer promised streetcar service, electric lights, sidewalks and tree-lined roads. The neighborhood’s name came from a contest won by Wilmington Star circulation editor Montrose Bain, whose prize was ten dollars. Many houses followed in 1940–1943 as the North Carolina Shipbuilding Company expanded onto land intended for homes.
